trajectory_summary: The call moves quickly through verify and lands a booked phone appointment, but the rep's pace outruns the customer's comprehension — the customer has to ask what he's looking forward to and has to ask the company's name four minutes in. Energy is mixed: an appointment gets set, but the customer's late-call confusion suggests a fragile booking built on momentum rather than clarity.

observed_outcome.reasoning: A specific day (tomorrow) and time (4PM) were agreed for a phone appointment with a specialist. The mother, confirmed as a co-owner on the title at 01:03 under protocols.adult_child_decision_maker, is never invited or confirmed for that call, leaving the booking structurally vulnerable to a decision-maker gap at proposal stage.

bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: No utility bill amount or usage figure was ever requested or given. The rep instead states the design will be estimated off square footage ('since there isn't a lot of usage for the home, we'll just have to base it off square footage' at 04:17), bypassing the bill-anchor step entirely — plausible for a customer in the home under two months, but never explicitly framed as a deferred-to-closer item.

interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep never asks what interested the customer in solar. The closest thing to a motivation surfaces unprompted at 03:39 when the customer mentions his electric car, but this was customer-initiated late in the call, not drawn out by a verify question.

primary_coaching_focus.quote: Are you what's what's the name of the company, sir?
primary_coaching_focus.why: Carter never states the company name at open (00:03 is just 'Hi, this is Carter'), and it resurfaces four minutes later as a direct customer question after an appointment was already tentatively set. This is the single most consequential and clearest-to-replay gap on this call — a customer shouldn't have to ask who he's talking to after agreeing to a callback.

key_moments.stewart_read: The rep gives his first name only — no company name, no reference to the form submission, no state or legitimacy framing. This is a bare-minimum intro that leaves 'is this a scam?' unanswered at the point the schema says it must be resolved.

key_moments.quote: Some events, were, related to that home, so we cannot proceed with that.
key_moments.stewart_read: The customer references an unspecified negative event tied to solar at a previous home. This does not cleanly map to orphaned_flow (which is defined for customers with an existing, currently-owned solar system) since there is no indication this home ever had solar installed — it reads more like a vague past negative experience or blocked deal. There is no purpose-built schema section for this exact disclosure.

key_moments.quote: Cool. And then is your credit score above 670?
key_moments.stewart_read: Rep asks the correct threshold (670, matching schema) and accepts the stated 'yeah' at face value to qualify the lead forward. This is procedurally correct per the current script, but the schema itself flags that stated credit is an unreliable self-report (spencer_operator_note) — so this should be read as 'followed current procedure,' not as a proven-good decision independent of that open policy question.

key_moments.quote: So what I'm looking forward to?
key_moments.stewart_read: The rep had already moved to close the call ('Okay. K. Awesome. We'll talk to you then.') before the customer stopped him to ask what the appointment was even for. This shows the button-up recap was either skipped or so rushed the customer didn't absorb it.
